articles.title: A man destroyed a $60 million U.S. military plane at an Irish airport, prosecutors say
articles.summary: NEW YORK — An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said.
articles.body: NEW YORK — An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said. The man’s supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States’ involvement in Middle East conflicts. An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O’Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment. O’Corrain isn’t in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn’t been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf. The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won’t fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said. O’Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles (97 kilometers) southeast of Shannon. Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends “a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated.” An online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest of the U.S.’s war with Iran and support for Israel’s war in Gaza — a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians. “An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organizer Tracey Ryan wrote. O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, U.S. prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking onto the airport’s grounds, prosecutors said. He subscribed to a cellphone app that provided live flight tracking, including for military aircraft, and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminum, the primary material used to build the C-130, prosecutors said. He even tried to get in touch with someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon Airport, prosecutors said. “This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” James Barnacle, the head of the FBI’s New York office, said in a statement. O’Corrain attacked on April 11, breaching the airport’s perimeter at around 4:40 a.m. and breaking into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said. He used the crew’s hammocks to cover the plane’s windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed, the indictment said. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and putting ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said. O’Corrain laid waste to the plane over the next few hours, pulling, snipping and otherwise disabling its key components, the indictment said. He sliced wire bundles, crimped a liquid oxygen line, punctured air ducts and shattered every gauge in the cockpit, the indictment said. Had O’Corrain cut the oxygen line instead, he would’ve risked blowing up the plane, prosecutors said. Returning to the airport after resting elsewhere, the C-130 crew spotted O’Corrain through the uncovered cockpit at around 9:40 a.m. and alerted security, the indictment said. Crew members then saw him emerging through a roof hatch and swinging an ax at the plane’s exterior, according to the indictment, which included images taken from a video recording that show a man standing on the roof of the plane. O’Corrain then poured substances and objects into the fuel tanks, including ball bearings, before being arrested. Shannon Airport, which was used by President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a U.S. military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a U.S. military jet was parked.

O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, US prosecutors said, searching online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel.

articles.title: Pope Leo breaks silence on rosary striking his face in Peru, reveals details about cancer: 'Major surgery'
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV says his lung cancer was found in a routine check-up with no symptoms, crediting prayer and doctors for his recovery before the Peru trip.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV broke his silence Monday after being struck in the face by a rosary thrown by a worshipper in Peru, joking about the incident while also revealing details for the very first time about his cancer diagnosis and major surgery which took place before his recent trip to South America. The pope, who had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13, after doctors found a cancerous tumor, told reporters on the flight home to Rome that he has not fully recovered, but said he was determined to complete the long-planned 12-day journey. "Just over a month ago, as everybody knows, I underwent rather major surgery," Leo, 71, said during a roughly 45-minute news conference on board the papal plane returning from Lima, Peru. POPE LEO WELCOMED BACK AS HE DELIVERS ANGELUS PRAYER DAYS AFTER LUNG CANCER SURGERY "But from the very beginning, I had in mind that this trip had been planned and that I was going to make it happen." The pontiff credited his recovery to prayer, medical care and personal determination. "So, with God's help — and I firmly believe in the power of prayer, as I have literally received messages from all over the world — together with a certain personal determination, which I also have, and with the help of the doctors, it proved to be possible." Despite the demanding itinerary that included multiple flights and appearances before massive crowds in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, Leo acknowledged that he is still regaining his strength. POPE LEO XIV SEEN FOR FIRST TIME SINCE LUNG CANCER SURGERY AMID MAJOR RECOVERY MILESTONE "I must say that I am not at 100%, but I am doing quite well. Stamina is a gift I have received from the Lord," he said. The pope also revealed that his cancer diagnosis came as a shock after doctors found an abnormality during a routine annual medical examination. "The initial news came as a surprise. There were no symptoms — I felt fine," he said. "It was discovered during some medical tests, as part of what you might call a check-up: a routine annual examination that I have been having for many years." Leo said the abnormality initially appeared as a shadow on his lung before additional testing revealed a tumor. POPE LEO UNDERGOES BLOOD TESTS, X-RAY FOLLOWING CANCER SURGERY, VATICAN SAYS "A biopsy then confirmed that it was a tumor," he said, before adding that he had decided to get it done "right away." "By the grace of God, I remained calm," he added. The surgery removed the lower lobe of his right lung after doctors diagnosed lung adenocarcinoma, a type of lung cancer. The pope was discharged four days later. "No further treatment is necessary. However, as a precaution, I will need to continue having these routine check-ups, simply to keep an eye on things, as is normal," he explained. The Vatican cleared the pontiff to move forward with his South American trip after medical evaluations in late October. The journey, which began Nov. 6, marked Leo's first papal visit to Latin America. He also holds Peruvian citizenship and spent roughly two decades serving as a missionary and bishop in Peru before taking on leadership roles at the Vatican. POPE LEO XIV HIT IN THE FACE BY FLYING ROSARY DURING FAREWELL MASS IN PERU, VIDEO SHOWS It was while riding in the popemobile through huge crowds toward the Mass in Lima on Nov. 16 that Leo was struck near the eye by a rosary thrown from the crowd. "The affection shown by the Peruvian people, including the person who, with such great faith, simply wanted to offer me a rosary, is something one carries in one's heart — or perhaps in one's eye," he joked about the incident. "These are experiences that leave a lasting mark on one's life." "Some even tried to get past the National Police barricades. They simply wanted to live, feel, and experience this faith," he said.

articles.title: 8-year-old detained by ICE in San Diego released from custody
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security previously confirmed that ICE agents placed the child in federal care after he attended a check-in appointment with a man...
articles.body:
An 8-year-old Haitian boy who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this month in San Diego has been released, according to an advocacy group and the boy's school.

"School leadership, and counselors had a meeting with the student when he returned to school this morning to ensure he had all the supports he and his family needed, and then he went off to class," the San Diego Unified School District said in a statement.

Haitian Bridge Alliance , which had advocated for the boy's release, said it welcomed the development.

"An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love—not in immigration detention," said Guerline Jozef, executive director of Haitian Bridge Alliance, in a statement. "We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry."

The Department of Homeland Security previously confirmed that ICE agents placed the child in federal care on Nov. 5 after he attended a check-in appointment with a man the agency said claimed to be the boy's uncle.

Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy, a third grader, has been living with relatives since his father was deported in 2025. In August of this year, following a legal victory for the Trump administration, some 350,000 Haitians living in the U.S. lost Temporary Protected Status , stripping them of deportation protections and work permits.

Advocates recorded and documented the moment when the 8-year-old was escorted by at least one ICE agent inside the Edward J. Schwartz building in San Diego, with Haitian Bridge Alliance saying the detention left the boy's cousins "in tears."

DHS said at the time that the agents designated the child an unaccompanied minor because "the alleged uncle could not establish legal guardianship of the minor."

"Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child's safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," DHS added.

The Office of Refugee Resettlement is an agency within the Department of Health and Human Services that is responsible for housing minors who lack a valid immigration status and who are taken into custody without their parents or legal guardians.

Haitian Bridge Alliance said in a previous statement that "when parents are taken into custody by ICE, they are not provided an opportunity to return home to see their children or to be able to transfer guardianship."

"ICE just incarcerated then deported without taking into account the wellbeing of the children left behind," it said.

articles.title: Rubio says tech outages are not part of 'systemic attack' against US
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" supporting theories online that recent disruptions affecting Microsoft, banks and flights are connected.
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.

Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot.

"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."

Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple.

Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor.

Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.

Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.

He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people.

"Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.

Technology-related disruptions have happened almost daily since Thursday, when a Microsoft outage disrupted many of its services, including email.

The next day, the US Federal Aviation Administration halted flights across the US for more than four hours with a rare national ground stop. It was the longest halting of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US.

The US transport secretary said the issue was technical and caused by a copper wire upgrade and outdated equipment.

On Monday, a United Airlines technology failure delayed about 150 flights and a JPMorgan Chase software problem disrupted service at the biggest and most utilised banks in the US.

Both United and Chase said a software issue was behind the glitch.

Apple users were impacted by outages affecting iCloud and Apple Pay on Tuesday. The company said the cause was not a cyber-attack but the outage was triggered by an an internal update.

The same day, a highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications also went offline for a period of time.

Tech experts weigh in: 'No conspiracy here'

Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline, and bank disruptions from the last five days.

Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, acknowledged the circulating theories on social media linking the barrage of outages.

"There is no conspiracy here," he told the BBC.

"There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and it's now being asked to change very quickly."

Beevers said AI is only part of the story.

"It's putting more strain on these legacy networks, and it's also creating real urgency around security," he said.

"Our customers are the amazing teams behind these networks at airlines, banking, energy, and retail who are essentially doing heart surgery on a global scale to get these networks back up and running quickly."

Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Sherrod DeGrippo, said: "What this week really underscores is how tightly coupled, and fragile, our core digital infrastructure is, where a single software bug or router failure can cascade nationwide."

articles.title: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump
articles.summary: Asif Merchant was found guilty in March of trying to hire undercover FBI agents as hitmen to assassinate US officials, including the president.
articles.body:
A Pakistani man with ties to Iran's government has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in a plot to assassinate US President Donald Trump and other officials.

Asif Merchant was found guilty in March of attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire after trying to hire hitmen to kill Trump, former President Joe Biden, and former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley.

The hitmen were instead undercover FBI agents.

In court, he said he was acting under the direction of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to avenge the 2020 US assassination of Qasem Soleimani, Iran's topmost military commander.

New York US federal judge Eric Ross Komitee sentenced Merchant on Tuesday to 330 months (27 years and six months) in prison, months after a jury handed its guilty verdict.

Although other US officials were potential targets, the assassination plot was largely focused on Trump because he was president at the time Soleimani was killed. Trump has spoken publicly about ordering the US airstrike that killed the Iranian general while he was travelling in Iraq.

In response to the killing, Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said "severe revenge awaits the criminals" behind the attack.

Prosecutors said Merchant initially travelled to Iran for religious pilgrimages and he was then introduced to an IRGC handler. He travelled to Iran 15 times where he received training from Iranian intelligence officers, prosecutors said, before flying to the US in April 2024 to carry out the plot.

Prosecutors said Merchant paid $5,000 to the undercover hitmen as part of an initial payment. He was arrested in July 2024 in Texas as he was about to leave the US.

In court, Merchant argued that he "had no other option" than to go along with the plot because his handler indicated that he knew who Merchant's Iranian relatives were and where they lived.

He said he had anticipated being arrested before anyone was killed and intended to cooperate with the US government, CBS, the BBC's US partner reported. He had hoped that would help him obtain a green card.

The jury deliberated for less than two hours before returning its verdict, US media said.

"An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

"The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable."

articles.title: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
articles.summary: The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless vehicles from operating on the state's highways following a series of traffic incidents.
articles.body:
Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.

The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.

California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".

In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".

A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."

Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.

Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.

The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.

In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.

In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia , in the early hours of the morning.

articles.title: 'Human': Cambridge’s 'word of the year' is a counterbalance to AI
articles.summary: The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ its Word of the Year for 2026, reflecting a growing debate over what distinguishes people from artificial
articles.body: The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ its Word of the Year for 2026, reflecting a growing debate over what distinguishes people from artificial intelligence (AI) as machines become increasingly capable of performing tasks once considered uniquely human.The choice highlights how the rapid spread of AI has prompted people to reconsider the value of human creativity, judgement, emotion and connection. It also points to a change in the way the word is being used, with expressions such as ‘human-written’, ‘human-generated’ and ‘human-made’ increasingly distinguishing work produced by people from content created by AI.Cambridge Dictionary defines ‘human’ as having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines.Why ‘human’ Cambridge Dictionary said the growing presence of AI in everyday life had led to a renewed appreciation of the human element in what people consume and experience.Colin McIntosh, chief editor of Cambridge Dictionary, said: “Artificial intelligence has been a growing presence in society for years now, but this year it seemed to be everywhere. In many areas of life this has led to a re-evaluation of what it means to be human, as a counterbalance to AI.”He added that 2026 had been marked by a renewed appreciation of the human factor and a greater value being placed on human involvement in everyday life. The dictionary said its analysis of language data, internet trends and search habits supported the selection.One of the clearest signs of this shift is the growing use of the word ‘human’ to identify the origin of creative work. As AI-generated writing, images, music and videos become more common, businesses and creators are increasingly highlighting when something has been made by a person.Cambridge described this as a ‘human premium’, the added value people may attach to a product or experience because they know it involved human effort, judgement and craftsmanship. In a marketplace increasingly filled with AI-generated material, the imperfections and personal involvement associated with human work can become part of its appeal.‘Human’ was selected from a shortlist that included ‘agent’, ‘analogue’, ‘wholesome’ and ‘chic’.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rafael Grossi is eyeing the UN’s top job. Will US support nuke his chances?
articles.summary: The nuclear watchdog chief is seen as technically competent, but questions remain about his plans for UN reform.
articles.body:
International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) chief Rafael Grossi is eyeing the position of United Nations secretary-general amid a tense race to replace Antonio Guterres.

The Argentinian nominee has finished second in the latest UN Security Council (UNSC) straw poll behind Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan , with nine “encourage” and four “discourage” votes and eight candidates still in the fray.

Grossi, 65, has earned admiration and criticism in equal measure for his IAEA tenure, defined by his hands-on approach to crisis diplomacy in active war zones, but also by accusations of partisanship, levelled against him, especially by Iran.

He is running on an agenda to reform the UN in a way seen as favourable to United States President Donald Trump and his political ally, Argentinian President Javier Milei.

But China and Russia – two of the five permanent UNSC members with veto power – are unlikely to back a candidate so closely aligned with Washington, analysts say, and a global civil society campaign is throwing its weight behind the selection of the first woman to lead the UN in the organisation’s 81-year history.

Grossi’s legacy at the IAEA and decades-long career as an Argentinian diplomat have cast him as a pragmatic crisis manager.

Since being appointed the UN nuclear watchdog’s director general in 2019, Grossi has been firmly in the front row in moments of international tension, including personally leading inspection teams to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Chornobyl nuclear power plants after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Jan Wouters, professor of international law and international organisations at KU Leuven in Belgium, said Grossi has “transformed the technical watchdog into a highly visible, proactive, diplomatic actor”.

“[He] significantly elevated the agency’s global profile through constant shuttle diplomacy and direct engagement with world leaders,” Wouters told Al Jazeera.

In Ukraine, by “focusing on technical safety rather than territorial sovereignty, he successfully brokered eight localised ceasefires between Russia and Ukraine to allow critical plant repairs” during the war, he added.

However, Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez, adjunct professor at the Pompeu Fabra law faculty in Barcelona, Spain, said Grossi’s very active role has “angered” the veto-wielding Russia, which sees him as having overstepped his position as agency head.

To be elected to lead the UN, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour from the 15-member UNSC while avoiding a veto from any of its five permanent members (P5) – China, France, Russia, the US, and the United Kingdom. The 193-member UN General Assembly (UNGC) then has to sign off on the final choice.

The race is coming down to the wire, as Guterres must leave his post on December 31.

While none of the P5 has publicly announced its preference, the South China Morning Post reported that Beijing has ruled out Grossi for being too close to Washington and would instead back Grynspan.

While Iran is not a member of the UNSC, it has also been vocal in its opposition to Grossi as UN secretary-general. Tehran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, accused the IAEA this month of being overly influenced by the US and European countries in its “one-sided and biased reporting about Iran’s peaceful nuclear programme”.

The IAEA has estimated that Iran was holding 440.9kg (972lb) of uranium enriched to up to 60 percent before the June 2025 Israeli-US attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities. While uranium must be enriched to 90 percent to become weapons-grade, the process becomes quick at 60 percent. The amount Tehran has would be enough, if enriched further, to build 10 nuclear weapons, according to the agency.

Jimenez Martinez said Grossi is likely to withstand the criticism, “because the majority of governors of the [IAEA] agree with his approach on Iran”.

“In the context of the UN, probably [this will lead to] a bit of fireworks, but I don’t think it will change many votes,” he said.

Grossi’s technical ability to lead the UN alone is unlikely to put him much ahead in the race, observers said. Candidates for the post of secretary-general must also be seen as defenders of the UN Charter and the UN’s international law and human rights instruments.

For this reason, support from the Argentinian president is seen as Grossi’s main liability. Milei has framed international institutions as threats to national sovereignty and individual liberty, describing the UN itself as “useless” and its diplomats as “fatally arrogant parasites”.

Since being elected president in 2023, Milei has reignited a longstanding dispute with the UK over the Falkland Islands , a British-administered territory over which Argentina claims sovereignty. Milei has told UN delegates that the principle of self-determination should not apply to the population of the islands, which Argentina calls Las Malvinas.

The Trump administration has also been a fierce critic of the UN, withdrawing Washington from key agencies, slashing UN funding and bypassing the body when it came to launching the war on Iran in February.

Jimenez Martinez said Grossi is seen as close to both Milei and Trump and as someone who could usher in a UN agenda aligned with their foreign policies.

“This will mean, in practice, a shrinking of the UN structure,” Jimenez Martinez said, including merging agencies and reorienting the body around security rather than development.

Grossi has called on world leaders to have the “courage to reform” the institution and lead it into a new era. According to Jimenez Martinez, his insistence on cutting red tape while failing to elaborate on safeguards is unlikely to get him a green light from the UNGA.

Alvina Hoffmann, senior lecturer in diplomatic studies at SOAS University of London, said Grossi is widely seen as a candidate whose “emphasis is on improving the system and cutting overlapping mandates, rather than addressing the structural drivers of inequality”.

He is also seen as someone who focuses on personal leadership, confidential negotiations and preventive diplomacy, “rather than issuing public declarations or condemnations”, which “might come at the expense of being able to call out violations of international law at a time in which international law is increasingly under attack”, Hoffmann said.

According to the tradition of geographical rotation, the UN secretary-general post should next go to a Latin American. Five women are running in the race, and public and civil society pressure is at an all-time high to elect the first woman to the post.

Ben Donaldson, adviser to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, a civil society movement advocating for the appointment of the first female secretary-general, said that while electing the next UN chief should be based on merit, this criterion “is not inconsistent with gender considerations”.

UNGA “resolutions and international standards affirm that due regard should be given to achieving gender balance in senior UN leadership”, Donaldson told Al Jazeera.

“In applying these principles, member states should assess candidates not only on their individual competencies and experience, but also on how their personal characteristics and professional trajectories contribute to a leadership that reflects the diversity of the international community.”

“The United Nations has existed for 80 years without ever appointing a woman as secretary-general,” he added. “This persistent imbalance stands in contrast to the organisation’s own commitments to equality, parity and nondiscrimination.”

articles.title: Locals and council to fight Norfolk data centre and solar farm
articles.summary: Those behind the plans say it will provide a more secure energy system and vital AI infrastructure.
articles.body:
Plans to build one of England's largest solar farms and a huge data centre have been described as "extremely oppressive" for an agricultural landscape.

Some 550 people watched a King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council meeting on Monday, which was also livestreamed, to discuss the infrastructure projects near King's Lynn, Norfolk.

The Longmarsh Green Energy (LGE) developments would cover 4,695 acres (1,900 hectares) of farmland across two sites.

A spokesperson said it would "make an important contribution" to energy systems and supporting online networks.

The council opposed the scheme's approval.

However, owing to the development's scale, it will be deemed a nationally significant infrastructure project, which means its approval will rest with the government rather than the local authority.

Karen Stone, 62, who raised her family in Tilney St Lawrence, Norfolk, said she was "absolutely shocked" by the plans for a data centre and solar farm, especially "the noise, the size of it".

She said: "We made a choice to live here because we watch all the agriculture all through the year.

"And in the last five years, while we've had all of this drought, they've had no drop in yield.

"We heard tonight, if you take all of the land they're talking about, [that's] 25 million loaves.

"We'll want to be paying five or six pound a loaf, will we? When we can't actually get any of that because we don't have the land?"

Lindy O'Dwyer, 66, agreed that data centres should not be built on "prime agricultural land. They can go elsewhere."

She said: "I feel very passionate about it. I'll be asking what next can I do as a person," to oppose the schemes.

Paul Rugg, 60, who also attended the meeting, said: "There's just so many better sites.

"Take a look at France where they're putting solar panels over car parks on top of buildings, you know? It's ludicrous."

Councillors voted unanimously against the schemes and agreed to make five recommendations including writing to the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, asking for local communities to "be at the heart" of planning decisions.

It also said it would evaluate any final government decisions, including pursuing any legal challenges.

Independent councillor, Simon Ring, who is also the authority's deputy leader, said he was a "fan of data centres" in the right place.

"They should be attached to swimming pools, to schools, to villages that have just been constructed," he said.

"Share that heat that's been thrown out into the atmosphere.

"Or better than that, help with our food security. Put a whole stream of greenhouses next to it so we can have all year our food.

"They do that in other parts of this world . Why we're not learning from that is beyond me."

Another councillor, Independent Jo Rust, who is the cabinet member for people and communities, believed the solar panel scheme was a "Trojan horse idea to get the data centre on board".

"And I think for the residents that do live in that area, it's going to be incredibly oppressive," she said.

James Kitchen is a fourth generation farmer. His 600 acre (242 hectares) family farm in Tilney-cum- Islington would border the proposed data centre and solar farm.

The land would also have three pylons crossing the edge of his fields.

Kitchen said: "I'm devastated about the whole thing. Worried about the compulsory purchase, worried about myself, my family."

He said his business uses data, explaining: "It's not what they're proposing here, it's the scale.

"We cannot afford to lose this highly productive land," said Kitchen.

"It is vital for the sake of national food security that this land remains producing food."

He said he was "delighted" councillors voted unanimously to oppose the schemes with no speakers in favour, and said they would "continue fighting .. we won't stop".

Natural England, a public body that advises the government, classifies the affected area as grade one, which means it is "excellent quality agricultural land".

Demand for data centres is increasing, partly driven by AI needing more processing power.

At the moment, there are about 477 data centres across the UK and construction researchers Barbour ABI thinks that will increase by about 100.

Most of them will be in London and the south east of England.

The government's Data Centre Covenant says: "Countries that can host and power data centres will ensure their sovereignty, strengthen economic resilience, and be better placed to capture the benefits of the digital economy, and help shape the future of AI."

A spokesperson for LGE said: "Longmarsh Green Energy will make an important contribution to helping the UK build a cleaner, lower cost and more secure energy system as well as supporting the online networks we all rely on - from emails, banking and streaming services to national defence and our NHS records.

"We recognise the importance of local community input into the design of our proposals and are currently consulting on the project prior to submitting a Development Consent Order application."

A public online consultation on the west Norfolk project is open until 26 November.

An application is due to be submitted by April 2027.

It could take six months for the plans to be examined by the Planning Inspectorate and a decision could be made by July 2028.

articles.title: What’s in the air you breathe? How to stay safe during smog season
articles.summary: India and Pakistan had 42 of the world’s 50 most polluted cities in 2025. Millions now face another toxic winter.
articles.body:
As winter approaches in the Northern Hemisphere, so does smog season, and few places are hit harder than South Asia.

Cities across the region, from New Delhi to Dhaka, are blanketed in a thick grey haze, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) exceeding 350 in several parts of India’s capital last week, a level classed as “hazardous”, according to the air quality monitoring platform IQAir.

In winter, a layer of warmer air can trap cooler air near the ground. Combined with low wind speeds, this stops pollution from vehicles, industry and crop burning from dispersing.

Al Jazeera visualises which cities have the worst air quality, how it is measured, how smog affects your health and what you can do to protect yourself.

Smog mostly comes from burning fossil fuels, particularly coal, along with exhaust from vehicles and factories, and smoke from forest and crop fires.

Summer smog and winter smog form differently. In summer, sunlight reacts with nitrogen oxides and other pollutants to form ground-level ozone. In winter, a layer of warm air can sit on top of cooler air near the ground, trapping pollution and stopping it from dispersing.

In South Asia, winter smog is made worse by geography. The Indo-Gangetic Plain, which stretches across parts of Pakistan, northern India, Nepal and Bangladesh, is one of the world’s most polluted regions. Hemmed in by the Himalayas to the north, the plain has weak winds and a shallow layer of air in winter, so pollution has nowhere to go.

The air we breathe is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, but it also contains small amounts of other gases and tiny particles, some of which are harmful.

Monitoring stations track six main pollutants, including ozone, nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter (PM), tiny particles suspended in the air.

The most harmful is PM2.5, particles 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter, about 30 times thinner than a human hair. They can travel deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

These readings are combined into an Air Quality Index (AQI). The US AQI runs from 0 to 500 and is split into six colour-coded categories:

Yellow (51-100) , moderate: acceptable for most people.

Orange (101-150) , unhealthy for sensitive groups: children, older adults and people with heart or lung conditions.

Red (151-200) , unhealthy: the general public may be affected.

Purple (201-300) , very unhealthy: health risks for everyone.

Maroon (301+) , hazardous: emergency conditions.

Which cities have the most polluted air?

All 50 of the world’s most polluted cities in 2025 were in Asia, according to IQAir, with 42 of them in India and Pakistan.

Loni, on the outskirts of Delhi in Uttar Pradesh state, topped the list with average PM2.5 levels of 112.5 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic metre), more than 22 times the WHO’s recommended limit, followed by Hotan in China and Byrnihat and New Delhi in India.

Vehicles account for 23 percent of Delhi’s winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20 percent, according to India’s Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The four Chinese cities on the list are in Xinjiang, where desert dust is a major source.

Air pollution, both outdoors and inside homes, is linked to about seven million premature deaths worldwide each year, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Pollutants mainly enter the body through the lungs, where they can cause inflammation, damage cells and weaken the immune system. PM2.5 can also pass into the bloodstream, reaching organs including the heart and brain.

Air pollution is most strongly linked to stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), lung cancer and pneumonia. It can also worsen asthma and reduce lung function, while smoke from cooking with fossil fuels indoors is linked to cataracts.

Long-term exposure has also been linked to dementia and a higher risk of diabetes.

Children, older people, pregnant women and those with heart or lung conditions are most at risk. Exposure during pregnancy has been linked to premature birth and low birth weight.

You can’t control the air outside, but these simple steps can reduce how much pollution you breathe in:

Wear a mask: Use a well-fitting N95 or similar mask outdoors, as cloth masks offer little protection against fine particles.

Keep indoor air clean: Close windows on high-pollution days and use an air purifier with a HEPA filter.

Limit outdoor activity: Avoid strenuous exercise outside on high-pollution days.

Check air quality: Check the Air Quality Index (AQI) in a weather app before going out.

Protect those most at risk: Take extra care with children, older people and those with asthma.

Governments are trying a range of measures to cut air pollution, particularly in large cities.

Car-free days close city centres to vehicles or limit driving by number plate. Paris held its first car-free day in September 2015, covering about a third of the city. Nitrogen dioxide levels fell by up to 40 percent in some areas, according to monitoring agency Airparif. From 2016, the city also began closing the Avenue de Champs-Elysees to traffic on the first Sunday of each month.

Low-emission zones charge the most polluting vehicles. Within three months of London’s Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) launching in 2019, nitrogen dioxide concentrations at roadside monitoring sites in central London fell by 19.6 percent, according to a University of Birmingham study.

Some cities have targeted household fuel burning. Krakow, Poland, replaced more than 25,000 coal and wood-burning heating devices before banning solid fuels for home heating in September 2019. Average annual PM2.5 levels in the city fell by 40 percent between 2010 and 2021, according to a 2025 study.

articles.title: Andy Burnham promises to 'move quickly' on Neets report
articles.summary: The prime minister tells the BBC he wants to get "stuck in" after the Milburn report proposes wide-ranging changes to help unemployed young people.
articles.body:
The prime minister has said he wants to "move quickly" on implementing recommendations in Alan Milburn's report on work and young people.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Andy Burnham said: "This isn't about waiting forever and a long-off-promised reform, I want to get stuck into it right now."

Milburn's report urged more job support for under-25s, a shake-up of the benefits system, early intervention in schools and tax cuts for businesses hiring young people.

The government said it backed the review's principles and is expected to set out which proposals it will take on shortly.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was no need for "costly government schemes to fix Labour's own mistakes".

Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform

"We need to stop making it so expensive and risky to hire young people," she added.

Last year, the government asked Milburn, a former Labour minister, to do a review into the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet), which has now reached almost one million.

Burnham praised the report as a "landmark moment" adding: "This is not just a benefits reform, it's a whole society change he is calling for."

Asked what the number of young people not in education, employment or training should be by the next election, Burnham said he wanted the level to come down "as soon as possible".

He said he wanted 45-day work placements offered to every 16-18-year-old "who wants one" and was working on funding the places.

The government has also announced it will fully fund college places for everyone aged 16 to 18 in England for 2027/28.

The Association of Colleges said the money would allow its members to enrol thousands of extra students each year "confident in the knowledge that they will receive funding for them".

Burnham said he wanted to get the benefit bill down adding: "No one can be comfortable with the idea of hundreds of thousands of young people on benefits - nobody, not me, not anyone."

However, he added that it required "more than the crude cuts the other parties are offering".

"All of my experience says a 'names not numbers' approach that looks at the whole person, their housing, their debt, their mental health issues and creates a rounded response, that is proven to be more successful at getting people into work."

Out of work and not in college: How quickly could Milburn's plans help you?

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report

Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036

In his report, Milburn warned that employer National Insurance, wage costs, business rates and employment protections could be factors in deterring employers from hiring unexperienced young people.

"Fair pay, greater security and predictable hours matter," Milburn said, but added that the cost and complexity of hiring young people had increased "sharply".

On workers' rights, Burnham argued a balance had to be struck adding: "The more you strengthen employment security that creates more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in."

Asked if former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had made the situation worse by increasing the tax employers pay, the prime minister said the government had increased support for those hiring long-term unemployed people.

He also defended his reset with the EU, which could make it easier for young Europeans to work in the UK.

He argued that a closer relationship with the EU would help grow the economy, which would provide more opportunities for young people.

Attempts to change the welfare system under Sir Keir Starmer last year failed when Labour backbenchers refused to support the £5bn cuts to benefits, raising concerns about the impact on disabled people.

So far, there are few signs that Burnham's plans will trigger a similar backlash, although some Labour backbenchers and the Unison trade union have said the proposals on benefits could push young people into poverty.

Steve Darling, the Liberal Democrat work and pensions spokesman, said the government should "scrap the damaging job tax" and work with European countries to grow the economy.

Green Party MP Sian Berry urged the minister to "reject cuts" for young disabled people.

"One million young people need a leg up - one that does not come with the chair being kicked out from under them," she said.

Reform UK said immigration was the "elephant in the room" and called on the government to cut employer national insurance for British workers "so that young Brits are at the front of the queue for new jobs".

articles.title: Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform
articles.summary: There is hope his Neets report has created a case on benefits which MPs can back, writes political editor Chris Mason.
articles.body:
The prime minister describes Alan Milburn's report on jobs, training and benefits for young people as a "watershed moment".

In so doing, he is accepting Milburn's case for change and taking on the task of delivering it. Were ministers to actually manage that, it would amount to one of the most significant shake-ups of the welfare state in its history.

But the proposed timeframe for this stretches to a decade, which is another geological era in political terms, at least two general elections away.

Milburn is a deft operator. From a round of morning television and radio interviews, to addressing the cabinet, to releasing his report into the wild, he was still out and about on Tuesday evening in Westminster persuading, charming and cajoling those possibly in need of all three.

And this former MP, still every inch the politician, has an ongoing role - appointed the chairman of the government's new Youth Opportunities Unit.

The new job, which will report directly to Andy Burnham, is about tying together the myriad different aspects of change he is suggesting, involving multiple government departments.

And yes, it does mean a 68-year-old bloke becomes an early beneficiary of new employment prospects for the young.

But that glib observation apart, there is a hope that Milburn has gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reforms they can endorse. Or, to put it more bluntly, one not grounded in a specific objective to make benefits cuts to make the sums add up elsewhere.

Plus, him hanging around perhaps means he can be a useful lightning conductor for any forthcoming angst on Labour's benches – as having persuaded them of the big picture mission, the gritty reality of implementing it begins to take shape.

Burnham promises to 'move quickly' on Neets report

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report

The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis

As the prime minister puts it in an interview in the Times , the government wants to offer "a new social contract" for "the let-down generation".

And he tells the newspaper that the initial upfront cost of around £500m, for employment support in 2027-28, will come from existing government budgets, which will mean cuts to other things elsewhere in government.

"I've asked the cabinet to reprioritise," he said.

Crucially, if you are in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, many of the decisions around whether or not to press ahead with these ideas will be up to the devolved governments in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.

From the government at Westminster's perspective, the focus now will be drawing up the specific plans for implementing Milburn's ideas, having accepted the broad thrust of his argument.

A white paper will follow in the new year, and then legislation.

What we don't know yet and will be crucial to the next stage of this debate, is precisely who will be the perceived winners and losers, at least in the short term, of the proposed changes.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told me that "those with the most severe and lifelong disabilities where work is not a realistic prospect" should, as Milburn suggests, "get more support than they receive at the moment". But how will those in this category be defined?

McFadden also told me that for some of those facing "extra costs" associated with their circumstances "there will be an extra cost benefit that will make at least a contribution towards that".

Again, how will those in this category be defined?

There is too an emerging political argument, following remarks from Alan Milburn already seized upon by the Conservatives, that decisions taken by Labour in its first few years in power have made a difficult situation harder still for young people looking for work.

On page 66 of his report , Milburn says the Employment Rights Act 2025 "could have major implications at a time when the youth labour market is already weak".

Interestingly, on this point, the prime minister is willing to push back, telling BBC Breakfast that "there is a balance to be struck".

"It is important to consider on the other side of this that the more you strengthen employment security, that can create more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in," he says. "We're going to consider all of this in the round."

The big decisions, then, now sit on the prime minister and the work and pensions secretary's desks.

In accepting the magnitude of Milburn's diagnosis and proposed treatment, they are tacitly accepting too that it is their responsibility to deliver – or at least begin to deliver – on much of what he suggests.

Their success or otherwise will matter to this generation of young people and those that will follow – and to the sustainability of the benefits system in the years ahead.

articles.title: Surrey PCC warns about AI voice cloning scams ahead of Christmas
articles.summary: Lisa Townsend says scammers need just three seconds of a victim's voice to be able to replicate it.
articles.body:
Scams involving AI-generated voice cloning have become prevalent in recent months, according to Surrey's police and crime commissioner.

PCC Lisa Townsend demonstrated the technology with an AI replica of her voice amid efforts to educate the public about the dangers scammers pose - and to warn that anyone could be vulnerable, especially in the lead-up to Christmas.

Residents in Surrey say scammers who have targeted them have become "very sophisticated".

Townsend told BBC Radio Surrey : "We know that criminals are absolutely capable and willing to exploit new technology."

She added: "We talk about people being vulnerable, but we are all vulnerable in different moments.

"It's online, it's on your mobile phone, it's coming through your computers, and sometimes it's coming from your landline."

Townsend said that, in order to clone a victim's voice, scammers only needed three seconds of someone's voice to be able to use AI software to craft full sentences in their likeness.

Statistics from UK Finance released in an annual report in June show that £1.3bn was stolen by scammers in 2025.

More than four million cases of fraud in which money was stolen were reported in the same period - a 11% increase compared with 2024, and up by 31% on 2023.

Speaking in the Friary Centre in Guildford, Enid Jones told BBC Radio Surrey she thought she was "reasonably on board with what to look out for".

However, she added scams were "getting more sophisticated".

Mum-of-two Victoria Oso added: "I find myself overwhelmed sometimes and I can see how it would be easy to take advantage."

articles.title: Battery warning after Gateshead recycling centre fires
articles.summary: Manager Chris Gaffney says one fire, which broke out in a truck, was "pretty lively".
articles.body:
A recycling centre which has seen several fires break out this year is urging people to dispose of their electrical items responsibly.

There have been five recorded fires at GAP Group Recycling centre in Gateshead during 2026, which were caused by lithium ion batteries.

Vapes, powerbanks and electric toothbrushes are just some of the everyday items which contain the flammable batteries .

Manager Chris Gaffney said: "We've had four small fires on site and one in the back of a truck which was pretty lively, we were able to contain them safely and are prepared to do so, but they can be very dangerous."

He said: "There needs to be greater awareness around what we can and can't throw out, we're all maybe guilty of tossing away something we shouldn't but there is a real danger."

Statistics from the Recycle Your Electricals campaign, led by not-for-profit organisation Material Focus, show more than one in four fires (26%) now happen in bin lorries.

It estimates 2,839 battery fires across the UK in 2025 were caused by items containing hidden batteries.

Bin lorries are usually checked with thermal scanners to pick up any devices or items which contain batteries. If the thermal scanners miss any of the items, staff check individual loads to ensure the batteries do not make it into the recycling process.

The campaign said 969 million electrical items and loose batteries were wrongly thrown away over the past year, including more than 196 million vapes.

Gaffney said staff had to sort through "a lot" of vapes.

"Our staff will pick through them and remove the batteries before they are recycled.

"The pincer which we use to pick up the material can easily puncture a battery - once that happens, it could easy go up and set off another battery and be a big problem."

Lithium ion batteries can ignite within seconds when crushed or damaged, creating fires that are notoriously difficult to extinguish.

articles.title: Investing £10m in Capitol Theatre a 'no brainer', says Horsham council
articles.summary: The refurbished Capitol Theatre will open on 29 November with a production of Dick Whittington.
articles.body:
Investing £10.2m in refurbishing a West Sussex theatre which first opened in 1936 has been described as a "no brainer" by councillors.

In 2024, Horsham District Council outlined plans to give the Capitol Theatre its first renovation in 23 years by increasing capacity, improving accessibility and giving the bar area and box office a makeover.

Works which began in January after the project was rescoped to reduce costs have now concluded, with the doors set to open once again on 29 November.

Cabinet member for wellbeing, culture and green spaces Anthony Frankland said investing in the arts always yielded an "enormous payback".

He said: "We're really lucky that the council here in Horsham has got the vision to make this investment, in what is really one of our, probably our best, community asset."

The Capitol, which opened in Horsham as The Ritz Cinema, was first acquired by the council in January 1982.

After 23 years without significant refurbishment, the council's community services manager, Nick Jenkins, said it was time for a refresh.

"I always say, 'it [the Capitol] was held together with love and sticky tape'. Behind the scenes, this venue needed real love and attention."

Jenkins said improving accessibility had "always been a key part of this project".

A modified row of 13 seats, which are all removable, has been added to give wheelchair users a choice about where to sit.

Smart glasses, which bring up subtitles for the production in any font, size or language, will also be available.

A changing places facility, which includes a shower and adult changing table, had also been installed for those with "profound needs", said Jenkins.

The first production at the revamped venue will be the 2026 pantomime, Dick Whittington.

Louie Spence, who will play Peppe Puss, said: "I'm very much looking forward to our show being the first show after the refurbishment."

articles.title: How the Houthis fund war effort and tighten grip on Yemen
articles.summary: The Houthis’ expanding war economy fuels military recruitment while poverty deepens and public services deteriorate.
articles.body:
Sanaa, Yemen – Mohammed, 19, joined the fighting on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in March this year, battling alongside Houthi forces. The fighting has been relentless over the past few months, as the Houthis advance. The Houthis have faced pro-government forces, as well as Saudi-led coalition air strikes.

They have also faced international sanctions and attempts by Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government to restrict their access to funds.

And yet, speaking during a recent visit to Sanaa, Mohammed said the Houthis were able to continue getting supplies to their fighters.

“It is not always war and death on the battlefield. We have a good time. We eat the best food. We can chew khat. If injured or sick, we will be taken care of. Our commander on the ground makes sure we have the supplies we need,” Mohammed told Al Jazeera.

Throughout a decade of war, Yemen’s Houthi group has developed a range of funding streams, which have enabled it to finance its military operations and tighten its grip on areas under its control.

The Mokha Center for Strategic Studies said in a July report this year that the Houthi financial system generates direct and indirect financial resources and costs worth approximately $2.5bn annually.

That includes around $800m from taxes and customs, $600m from additional fees and levies, $300m from cash and in-kind contributions to the war effort, and about $100m linked to mobilisation events, according to the report.

A May research paper from the same institution estimated that nearly 60 percent of collected revenues in Houthi-controlled areas are directed to the security and military sectors.

As the Houthis’ war grinds on against Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi-led coalition forces, Houthi authorities have employed more fund-generating techniques. Ali Naji, a Sanaa resident, often receives messages on his mobile phone, urging him to contribute to the missile and drone air forces.

“I do not contribute, but thousands of people do, even with 100 Yemeni riyals [$0.19 at the exchange rate set by Houthi authorities in Sanaa]. When these small contributions add up, they make millions, and this funds the war efforts,” Naji, a father of three, told Al Jazeera.

Another method is distributing envelopes to solicit contributions. Last week, Naji was watching the funeral procession of more than 40 civilians who were killed in Sanaa in what the Houthis said were Saudi air strikes.

A Houthi member approached him and handed him an envelope, requesting that he give a voluntary contribution to the war effort. “I did not feel comfortable refusing or returning it empty. I put 1,000 Yemeni riyals (around $1.90) inside the envelope and gave it back.”

When mass rallies are held, a large sheet of cloth is spread on the ground, and people can contribute what they can. “Some give cash. Some donate weapons such as rifles and pistols, or jambiyas [traditional daggers]. From one rally, millions of Yemeni riyals can be raised,” said Naji.

In addition, imported oil has been a major source of revenue for the Yemeni group. In January, the US Department of the Treasury said the Iranian government sold and provided a free monthly shipment of oil to the Houthis using Iranian-owned or affiliated companies based in Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates.

With the shipments of Iranian oil, the Houthis continued to acquire a significant amount of revenue through illicit oil sales, generating over $2bn annually, according to the US Department of the Treasury.

Yazeed Al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Houthis have established a self-reinforcing system in which “economic control finances coercion, and coercion enables further economic control”.

Their income sources include taxes, customs duties, zakat religious levies, and additional levies, and fuel and telecommunications, said Al-Jeddawy.

“Their control over import permits, fees, and access to foreign currency also gives them considerable leverage over traders and businesses. These resources sustain the security apparatus and patronage networks through which the movement enforces compliance and consolidates its authority,” he added.

Al-Jeddawy noted that the Houthi financial system supports recruitment amid shrinking employment opportunities and unpaid public-sector salaries.

“Joining Houthi forces has become one of the few sources of income available to some young men. Recruitment is accompanied by ideological indoctrination, extending the movement’s influence from military camps into families and local communities. Economic deprivation therefore does more than facilitate mobilisation: it helps the group militarise everyday life and reinforce their authority at the social level.”

A 2024 United Nations panel of experts estimated that Houthi fighters numbered around 350,000 , bolstered by the recruitment of fighters sometimes aged under 18.

These resources fund more than recruitment and mobilisation. “The group has expanded its security apparatus, developed increasingly sophisticated weapons, and invested in fortifications, trenches, tunnels, underground facilities, and weapons workshops. This level of continuous militarisation requires considerable and sustained expenditure,” said Al-Jeddawy.

Wafiq Saleh, an economic researcher and executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, said Houthi-run civilian institutions are starved of funds, salaries are not paid regularly, and basic services, such as health and education, continue to deteriorate.

“About one million Yemeni public employees have not received their salaries regularly since 2016. Meanwhile, the group has developed its arsenal and funded its war efforts. When war is a priority, the living conditions of the population become miserable,” Saleh told Al Jazeera.

Roughly 80 percent of the population in Yemen lives below the poverty line, and nearly 22.3 million people depend on some form of humanitarian assistance, according to United Nations reports.

For Mohammed, the Houthi soldier, funding military operations is “a duty” and “a long-term investment”.

“Liberating the country and expelling foreign forces is not free,” said Mohammed. “So, funding fighters and military operations should be every patriot’s priority.”

articles.title: Africa’s economic future cannot depend on Washington
articles.summary: Trump’s move to exclude South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA shows why Africa must accelerate its own economic integration.
articles.body:
On September 2 , United States President Donald Trump signed legislation extending the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) through the end of 2028, following overwhelming support in Congress. Yet just two months later, on November 2 , his administration announced plans to terminate the eligibility of South Africa and Rwanda for the programme from January 1, 2027.

The decision lays bare the fundamental weakness of AGOA: African economies depend on trade privileges that Washington can withdraw whenever its political priorities change.

AGOA is a US trade law that currently covers 33 eligible sub-Saharan African countries. It was enacted on May 18, 2000, to allow these countries to export thousands of products to the US market duty-free, and was promoted as a strategic mechanism to foster economic growth, expand trade between the US and the continent and encourage economic and political reforms.

AGOA initially delivered promising results. It is estimated to have supported more than 300,000 direct jobs across Africa and 1.3 million indirect jobs. According to a 2024 US Trade Representative report, two-way goods trade between the US and sub-Saharan Africa reached $47.5bn in 2023, including $9.7bn in imports under AGOA and the Generalized System of Preferences (GSP), of which $5.5bn consisted of non-oil products such as apparel and agricultural goods.

However, recent figures point to growing challenges, with some even suggesting a decline. A Congressional Research Service report shows that US imports receiving AGOA duty-free treatment dropped sharply from $7.9bn in 2024 to $5bn in 2025. Another analysis by the German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS) noted that the share of US imports from sub-Saharan Africa benefiting from AGOA and GSP preferences plummeted from more than 80 percent in 2008 to roughly 24.7 percent in 2021 amid eligibility uncertainty and short renewal windows.

Only a few eligible sub-Saharan African countries capture most of the programme’s benefits. South Africa is its largest beneficiary, with exports to the US worth billions of dollars annually, while most other eligible countries struggle to make full use of its preferences.

Furthermore, because the US administers the programme’s preferences unilaterally, rather than through a bilateral treaty, Washington can exclude or reinstate any eligible country based on its own assessments and criteria, including market reforms, human rights and labour standards.

Since the programme’s inception, some countries suspended from AGOA have criticised the impact of their removal. Ethiopia’s suspension in 2022, for instance, led to the loss of thousands of garment sector jobs.

In practice, Washington’s geopolitical interests often carry more weight in eligibility decisions than AGOA’s stated criteria.

The Trump administration’s decision to terminate South Africa’s and Rwanda’s AGOA eligibility is a clear case in point. Both countries have pursued policies that conflict with Washington’s interests and that the administration regards as a threat. South Africa has strengthened its economic and political ties with US rivals such as China and Russia, while facing accusations from Washington of obstructing American trade and investment, alongside Trump’s allegations of a “white genocide”.

Rwanda’s alleged support for the M23 rebel group in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has also brought it into conflict with US interests in the region’s critical minerals.

Sharp declines in AGOA import values, unstable US trade policies, and short-term extensions leave African exporters highly vulnerable. Losing AGOA access triggers immediate customs setbacks, including tariff increases of 15 to 20 percent on some products. Ultimately, these unpredictable extensions prevent AGOA from building a self-sustaining African industrial base, making accelerated implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) an urgent priority for the continent.

Africa’s economic vision cannot remain hostage to changing administrations’ policies or unilateral decisions made abroad, as the continent needs to build strategic resilience and economic independence. The AfCFTA is a historic trade agreement signed under the auspices of the African Union (AU) on March 21, 2018, in Kigali, Rwanda, which officially entered into force on May 30, 2019, with trading beginning on January 1, 2021.

The agreement aims to bring African Union member states into a unified market of over 1.3 billion people, with a combined gross domestic product (GDP) exceeding $3.4 trillion.

Relying on a vast regional market would mitigate the impact of external shocks, such as the revocation of preferential trade agreements like AGOA or the sudden imposition of steep tariffs. Given that trade between African nations currently accounts for only about 15–18 percent of the continent’s total trade, the AfCFTA aims to progressively eliminate tariffs on 90 percent of tariff lines, thereby stimulating internal commerce and providing a buffer against declines in Western markets caused by tariff fluctuations.

AGOA and many other external agreements have largely kept Africa in the role of a raw material supplier. In contrast, the AfCFTA encourages the development of regional value chains, where one African nation might produce raw materials, another processes them into finished goods, and the final product is sold to consumers within the continent, with fewer tariff barriers.

AfCFTA has made notable progress in developing the instruments needed for continental trade. The number of countries participating in trade initiatives under the agreement has grown to include South Africa, Egypt, Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda and Tunisia, making use of its preferential tariff arrangements.

The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), launched on January 13, 2022, enables banks and financial institutions to conduct cross-border transactions in African currencies, reducing reliance on foreign currencies such as the US dollar.

The African Union also adopted protocols on competition policy in February 2023 and digital trade in February 2024, aimed at promoting fair competition and facilitating e-commerce. In August 2026, the AfCFTA Secretariat signed an agreement to modernise and digitise customs systems. The AfCFTA Adjustment Fund has also been activated, with an estimated financing requirement of $8bn–$10bn, to support developing countries and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as they adapt to the requirements of the single market.

For AfCFTA to serve its purpose and reduce dependence on volatile global trade agreements that prioritise Western interests over those of Africa, the continent still needs to accelerate economic integration by removing tariff and non-tariff barriers and harmonising trade and regulatory policies to facilitate the smooth movement of goods and services.

To improve local markets, African countries must undertake the costly and risky investments involved in building cross-border infrastructure to reduce the cost of moving goods and services between African countries. Digital energy grids will be essential to this infrastructure, alongside roads and railways.

Africa must shift from simply exporting raw materials to building strong regional value chains focused on local manufacturing and innovation. Meeting the needs of the continent’s vast market would strengthen its economic self-sufficiency and reduce its vulnerability to external political decisions and the expiration of unilateral trade agreements.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
