articles.title: In Maharashtra's Sindhudurg, 1,000 women farmers across 25 villages switched to a new rice-growing method on 100 hectares; UNDP field trials found yields around 58% higher than those from traditional plots
articles.summary: For decades, Supriya Gawade and Kavita Manjrekar have worked in the rice fields of Talekarwadi village in Maharashtra's Sindhudurg district.
articles.body: For decades, Supriya Gawade and Kavita Manjrekar have worked in the rice fields of Talekarwadi village in Maharashtra's Sindhudurg district. From preparing the land and sowing seeds to transplanting, weeding and harvesting, much of the work has fallen on women. But in recent years, farming has become more difficult. Labour is harder to find, wages and fertiliser costs have increased, and rainfall has become less predictable.Both women, now 65, decided to try a different way of growing rice. They are members of Streeshakti Mahila Gat, a collective of 20 women farmers that adopted the System of Rice Intensification (SRI) this season. The method changes how rice seedlings are planted and how water and nutrients are managed.Their experiment is part of a wider initiative in which 1,000 women farmers across 25 villages in Sindhudurg have adopted the method on a combined area of 100 hectares. According to a report by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) India, the initiative has recorded an average rice yield of 55.2 kg per 100 square metres under SRI, compared with 34.9 kg from traditionally cultivated plots. This represents an increase of about 58% in the field trials.Why the women decided to change how they farmSupriya grew up in rural Sindhudurg and began working in rice fields as a teenager. Kavita, in contrast, was born and raised in Mumbai before moving to the village in her forties and taking up farming.Both have experienced the physical demands of rice cultivation. In the UNDP report, Supriya explains that women handle almost every stage of the crop cycle, from May, when the land is prepared, until the October harvest. The work is carried out alongside household responsibilities.Kavita says their small plots, usually around 15 to 20 gunthas (approximately 0.15 to 0.2 hectares), depend heavily on manual labour, fertilisers and sufficient rainfall. Rising input costs and a shortage of workers have added to the pressure. She also points to changes in rainfall, which have made it harder to plan cultivation.When Kavita heard about SRI at a village meeting, she decided to test it. She and her daughter-in-law, Akanksha, were among the first in the collective to take up the method. They later encouraged other women in their neighbourhood to join.What is the System of Rice Intensification?SRI is a method of rice cultivation that changes the way seedlings are raised, planted and managed. Instead of transplanting four or five older seedlings together, farmers plant a single young seedling, around 14 days old. The plants are spaced about 25 centimetres apart in rows, allowing them more room to grow.The method also involves mechanical weeding and managing nutrients without keeping fields continuously flooded.According to the UNDP report, the wider spacing and careful management allow plants to develop more tillers, or stems that can produce grain-bearing panicles. The project's agriculture associate, Nutan Sawant, observed that SRI plants in the Sindhudurg fields developed an average of 20 to 25 tillers from one transplanted seedling. Conventionally grown plants produced around six to 12 tillers, despite being planted in groups of five or six seedlings.The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) has also documented the potential benefits of modified SRI. Its published technology note reports grain-yield increases of 36% to 49%, water savings of 22% to 35% and seed savings of about 90% compared with conventional transplanted rice. These figures come from separate research and should not be confused with the 58% increase recorded in the Sindhudurg field trials.How the women learnt to work togetherThe transition was not immediate. The women had followed conventional rice-growing practices for years and were unsure whether planting fewer seedlings farther apart would leave too much room for weeds or affect the crop.In the UNDP report, Akanksha recalls that several members initially questioned whether a single seedling would survive where they had traditionally planted four or five. Project workers Nutan Sawant and Yugandhara Kamble held meetings, explained the method and visited fields to address questions during the Kharif season.The collective also found ways to reduce dependence on hired labour. Instead of each farmer working only on her own plot, members organised group farming and helped one another in their fields. Akanksha coordinated schedules so that work could be completed at the right stage of cultivation. The women also created a WhatsApp group to share updates and observations.They made practical adjustments to suit local conditions. The lateritic and coastal alluvial soil in the area was damaging the blades of the cono weeders used to remove weeds between rows. The group modified the blades so the equipment could work better in their fields. They also developed a measuring scale marked at 25-centimetre intervals to help maintain the required distance between seedlings.As more women became interested, families who had migrated to cities offered their unused fields to the collective. The group took up cultivation on an additional eight hectares beyond the land its members already farmed.What the field trials foundThe results became clearer as the Kharif season progressed. According to the UNDP report, SRI plots were less affected by the rainfall deficit associated with El Niño conditions than conventionally cultivated plots. The wider spacing meant plants faced less competition for available water and nutrients.Crop-cutting experiments recorded an average yield of 55.2 kg per 100 square metres from SRI plots, against 34.9 kg from traditional plots. It means an increase of approximately 58%. The report also noted that SRI-grown rice was ready for harvest by early October, while some conventionally cultivated plots had not yet reached the harvesting stage. articles.title: Inside extravagant wedding of Anant Singh’s daughter: Helipads for VIPs, Jaipur-inspired pavilion, horse race
articles.summary: PATNA: A luxury Land Rover Defender for the bridegroom, a BMW for the bride’s younger brother, a horse race with an SUV as the top prize and a wedding
articles.body: PATNA: A luxury Land Rover Defender for the bridegroom, a BMW for the bride’s younger brother, a horse race with an SUV as the top prize and a wedding feast featuring more than 150 dishes — the wedding of Mokama MLA Anant Singh’s daughter is being planned on a grand scale.Preparations are under way at Singh’s ancestral village of Nadawan in Bihar’s Patna district, where hundreds of workers, artisans and decorators are working round the clock to transform a sprawling site into a wedding venue ahead of the November 25 celebrations.The wedding of Singh’s younger daughter, Shivangi Singh, to Rishikesh Kumar, alias Ankit, is expected to draw around four lakh guests. Rishikesh is the son of Ranvijay Kumar, a commandant from Krishnanagar in Bihta, Patna. He holds an MBA degree and has lived in the United States for around 11 years.Luxury cars and an elaborate wedding venueThe Land Rover Defender, estimated to cost between Rs 2.5 crore and Rs 3 crore, has already reached the village. The vehicle is for the bridegroom, while a BMW worth around Rs 1 crore has been arranged for Singh’s younger son, Abhinav, whose 'janeu' ceremony will take place alongside the wedding.The wedding venue is being developed across more than 10 bighas of land, with a separate ground spread over nearly 12 bighas being prepared for a horse-racing competition.One of the main attractions will be a stage and mandap inspired by Jaipur’s Patrakar Chowk. Measuring around 100ft in width, 35ft in length and 30ft in height, the structure is being built for the 'jaimala' ceremony.Flowers are being sourced from China and Bengaluru, while decorative materials are being brought in from different parts of the country. Workers have also been brought from Mau in Uttar Pradesh to complete the arrangements.Event manager and decorator Pradeep Jaiswal said 400-500 workers and artisans were involved in the preparations. Special lighting equipment has been brought in from Bengal. The pavilion will have restaurant arrangements at its centre, while food will be served at two locations to prevent overcrowding.Horse race with an SUV as top prizeA horse-racing competition, scheduled for November 25 from 2pm to 4pm, is expected to add to the celebrations. A specially prepared ground about 1km from Singh’s residence will host the event, with horses and riders invited from several states.The winner will receive an SUV, while the second and third-place finishers will get a motorcycle and a scooter respectively, according to Manish Kumar, an associate of Singh.Among the horses being prepared for the race is Ranchi Express, a Sindhi-breed horse owned by Mohammad Mahtab Ansari of Kanke in Ranchi. It was brought from Gujarat’s Kutch around 15 days ago and is being trained for the competition. Shekhawat Ali will ride the horse.A stable is also being constructed at Nadawan to accommodate the horses arriving for the event.Feast for lakhs of guestsFood is expected to be another major attraction, with the menu featuring more than 150 varieties of dishes. The preparations are expected to cater to around four lakh guests.The spread will include traditional Bihari preparations as well as dishes from other states. Sweets will include kaju katli and Silao khaja, a speciality from Nalanda known for its distinctive 52-layer structure.Five helipads are also being constructed for VIP guests.Political leaders among inviteesSingh has expressed his wish to invite Prime Minister Narendra Modi, former Bihar chief minister Nitish Kumar, RJD president Lalu Prasad and Tejashwi Prasad Yadav. Assembly Speaker Prem Kumar has already received an invitation.Singh has said there will be no political distinction among the guests and that visitors from anywhere in the world, including India and Pakistan, will be welcome.The celebrations will begin on November 20 with 'phaldan' and 'tilakotsav'. A 'Haldi Kalash' ceremony is scheduled for November 23, followed by 'mehndi' and 'sangeet' on November 24. The wedding and reception will take place on November 25, with dinner scheduled to begin at 7pm.Singh’s family has organised elaborate wedding celebrations in the past. His eldest daughter, Raj Nandini, married Puneet Kumar in 2015.“I was married to Raj Nandini, eldest daughter of Singh, in 2015. In my wedding, only parking was made on around 4 bighas of land,” said Puneet.He said the Defender was chosen by Shivangi and gifted to her on her birthday. She completed her schooling in Delhi and post-graduation from Delhi University.The celebrations are taking place as Singh faces a legal deadline in a separate case. articles.title: Hungry, unpaid and afraid: Africa’s journalists pushed to the brink
articles.summary: The exploitation of journalists is undermining independent reporting and the public’s right to know.
articles.body:
How can a hungry journalist be expected to deliver the facts the public needs? Across Africa, journalists are struggling to survive, working for months without pay and reporting without contracts or protection. This is not just a workplace crisis. It is an attack on the very conditions that make independent journalism possible.

Yet journalists are expected to expose corruption, scrutinise power and verify claims while wondering how they will pay for food, rent or transport to their next assignment. For many, journalism has become a struggle for survival. The consequences are visible in every delayed salary, every unpaid assignment and every story abandoned because the reporter cannot afford to pursue it.

With UNESCO’s support, the Federation of African Journalists (FAJ) and its affiliated unions and associations across Africa’s five regions carried out the first journalist-led, continent-wide survey of journalists’ working conditions, labour rights, safety and media freedom. It drew responses from 1,586 journalists in 45 African countries. Among those surveyed, 61 percent said their income from journalism did not meet their basic living needs, 58 percent reported delayed salaries and 62 percent had no written contracts.

Behind these numbers are journalists expected to perform an essential public service without the means to make a decent living. In Central Africa, 55 percent of respondents reported salary arrears lasting three to eight months within a single year.

The deprivation extends beyond pay. Many respondents also reported having no health insurance or paid leave. Freelancers and contributors are among the most exposed. Many lack contracts, predictable incomes and social protections yet are expected to produce regular work and take risks similar to those faced by newsroom staff.

This widespread precarity is corroding the quality of journalism. Investigations require time, travel, secure communications, access to documents and careful verification. Poverty and unpaid work deprive reporters of these basic tools. A newsroom under financial strain has less capacity to check claims, protect sources and follow a story beyond the first official statement. Stories are dropped. Errors are harder to catch. The public is left with a thinner, weaker account of events.

The consequences for information integrity are grave. The FAJ report describes journalists relying on side businesses, borrowed money and allowances from outside sources, including political “per diems”. This does not mean that journalists in precarious work are dishonest. It means poverty wages and financial exposure can create openings for outside interests to influence what gets covered and how. These conditions can allow “brown envelope” practices to flourish. When a journalist’s ability to survive depends on money from a person or institution with a stake in a story, independent reporting is placed under pressure.

The survey shows that these abysmal conditions are already shaping coverage. Eighty-four percent of respondents said they practised self-censorship frequently or occasionally. Sixty-nine percent said threats had led them to avoid certain stories. When a journalist fears losing an already inadequate income, censorship does not need to arrive as a formal ban. It can be the decision not to investigate because the personal cost feels too high.

The danger is physical as well as economic. Sixty-five percent of journalists who took part in the survey had experienced work-related threats or intimidation in the previous three years. More than half rarely or never felt safe reporting, and 78 percent said they had no workplace access to legal support. Journalists are sent to report on dangerous events and uncover uncomfortable truths that powerful interests would rather keep hidden, then are left to face the perilous consequences alone.

Online attacks deepen the crisis. Journalists reported online harassment, digital surveillance and hacking attempts, often without access to digital safety training. Female journalists face additional risks, including sexual harassment, online gender-based violence, unequal pay and exclusion from leadership. When women are driven out of public debate by threats, journalism loses their reporting and the public loses the perspectives they bring. The strain is also evident in journalists’ wellbeing: 44 percent reported frequent burnout, and 47 percent had considered leaving journalism.

The survey’s regional findings highlight delayed or inadequate pay in West, Central and Southern Africa and political intimidation, arrests and legal harassment in East and North Africa. There is no single African newsroom experience: In some places poverty is the most immediate threat; in others, repression and physical danger dominate. Often journalists face both.

Country examples also show that democratic credentials alone do not guarantee decent conditions. The report describes Ghana as having relatively strong democratic credentials yet cites research from 2023 finding that many media workers there earned as little as G500 cedis ($38.80) to 1,000 cedis ($77.61) a month. Freelancers often relied on transport reimbursements, commissions or sponsored content to survive. Elections and democratic institutions matter, but without labour rights, fair pay and protection from pressure, journalists can remain economically vulnerable even in a more open political environment.

There are, however, practical examples of progress. In Mauritania, a government decision in 2025 regularised 1,860 media workers at public media institutions after a sustained campaign by the Association of Mauritanian Journalists with the backing of FAJ and the International Federation of Journalists. These journalists gained permanent contracts, equal pay and benefits, medical coverage, paid leave and retirement benefits after more than 30 years of campaigning for professional and social recognition. In Morocco, a collective agreement signed in February 2023 and negotiated by the National Syndicate of Moroccan Journalists secured a net monthly salary increase of 2,000 dirhams ($201) for eligible journalists with more than four years of experience. These changes show how government action and collective bargaining can put real protections into journalists’ working lives.

Namibia offers another important lesson. Journalists in the survey still described long hours, unpaid overtime and stagnant salaries. But formal registration of the Namibia Media Professionals Union gave media workers a recognised way to organise and bargain collectively. This month, the union secured a substantially improved settlement for workers facing retrenchment at The Namibian newspaper. This does not resolve the wider crisis, but it shows how collective representation can defend workers’ rights in practice.

In Somalia, long one of Africa’s most dangerous countries for journalists, the National Union of Somali Journalists led the development of a national action plan on journalists’ safety adopted in September 2022 after consultations involving journalists, the government and international partners. It sets out a Somali-led framework to strengthen journalists’ safety, media freedom, access to information and protection for female journalists. Its adoption was an important step towards safer working conditions for journalists.

Across the continent, the African Union and its organs have also taken steps to address journalists’ safety and media freedom. Ambassador Bankole Adeoye, AU commissioner for political affairs, peace and security, has been a vocal advocate for media freedom and journalists’ safety and a leading voice in affirming that professional media are indispensable to democracy and good governance. Over the past three years, the AU Peace and Security Council has increasingly addressed Africa’s media environment. In October, it called for greater protection of journalists, action against impunity and stronger safeguards for access to information.

These examples show what governments, media organisations and multilateral institutions must do. Enforce labour protections. Pay wages on time. Provide written contracts, social protection and legal support. Protect the right to organise and bargain collectively. Treat freelance journalists as workers with enforceable labour rights. Investigate attacks and stop using laws to intimidate reporters. Democratic safeguards and labour protections must advance together. Neither can substitute for the other.

When journalists are forced to choose between pursuing the truth and securing their own survival, the public pays the price: Investigations go unfinished, abuses escape scrutiny and vital facts remain hidden. Fair pay, secure employment and safety are essential to media freedom and the public’s right to know.
